source_title: Six CBSE clarifications in seven months: Why can't the board get its rules right? - India Today
source_excerpt:
CBSE has issued at least six major rounds of clarifications since May 2026, covering digital evaluation, extra marks, the three-language policy, passing criteria and curriculum changes. With board exams approaching, a new Education Minister and a new CBSE chairperson, can students expect a more stable 2027?
The Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) has spent much of 2026 explaining its own rules. From digital evaluation and extra marks to the three-language formula, passing criteria and now another Class 9 curriculum revision, students and schools have had to keep up with a steady stream of clarifications.
The latest came on October 29. CBSE has revised its Scheme of Studies for the 2026-27 Class 9 batch, dropping three curricular components and explaining how vocational subjects could help students meet their Class 10 passing requirements.
This is not an isolated announcement. At least six major rounds of clarifications have emerged since May. With the 2027 board examinations approaching, a new Education Minister in place and a new CBSE chairperson taking charge, the question is whether 2027 will bring greater clarity or another year of changing instructions. SIX CLARIFICATIONS IN SEVEN MONTHS: WHAT CHANGED?
SIX CLARIFICATIONS IN SEVEN MONTHS: WHAT CHANGED?
Here is a look at six major instances when CBSE had to explain, modify or clarify its rules in 2026.
After complaints and questions about the new On-Screen Marking (OSM) system for Class 12 answer sheets, CBSE defended its digital evaluation process. It explained how stepwise marking worked and directed dissatisfied students towards its verification and re-evaluation process.
The controversy eventually led to the transfer of the CBSE chairman Rahul Singh and secretary Himanshu Gupta on June 2, followed by an inquiry into the procurement of OSM services.
2. June 4: How are extra questions counted?
Students who obtained scanned copies of their evaluated answer sheets noticed discrepancies between marks recorded in calculation sheets and the final totals.
CBSE subsequently clarified how marks would be calculated when students attempted extra questions, explaining the process used to award the best possible marks.
CBSE issued a detailed clarification on its three-language framework after its May 15 announcement made three languages compulsory for Class 9 students from the 2026-27 session.
The board explained transition arrangements, exemptions, foreign-language combinations and which batches would have to appear for a third-language board examination.
4. July 10: More questions about the third language
The June clarification was not the end of the matter. CBSE issued another set of implementation guidelines addressing what happens if students fail the third-language assessment, how schools should arrange teachers, what happens when families relocate and how learning resources would be provided.
5. October 3: Did Class 10 passing marks change?
Confusion over a curriculum document suggested that Class 10 students would need 33% separately in internal and external assessments.
CBSE clarified that there was no change. Students still need 33% overall after combining internal assessment and board examination marks.
6. October 29: Three subjects dropped from the curriculum
In its latest circular, CBSE removed Individuals in Society and Computational Thinking and AI modules from the current Class 9 batch. Environmental Education will also not be taught to this batch when it moves to Class 10 in 2027-28.
The board has also explained the vocational education and subject-replacement rules for these students. WHAT DOES THE LATEST CLASS 9 AND 10 CHANGE MEAN?
WHAT DOES THE LATEST CLASS 9 AND 10 CHANGE MEAN?
The October 29 circular applies to students currently in Class 9, who will appear for their Class 10 board examinations in 2028. It does not affect students appearing for their Class 10 boards in 2027.
Students will have five compulsory board examination subjects: two languages, Mathematics, Science and Social Science.
Vocational education, however, remains compulsory. Students can choose Kaushal Vikas, which will be assessed internally, or one of 22 skill subjects that will have a Class 10 board examination.
Here is an important provision: if a student fails Mathematics, Science or Social Science, marks in an eligible skill subject can replace the failed subject for calculating the result. Kaushal Vikas does not qualify for this replacement.
Similarly, an eligible additional language can replace a failed compulsory language, subject to CBSE's conditions.
The idea is to give students more flexibility , but it also adds another set of rules that schools and parents must understand. A NEW YEAR, A NEW CBSE?
There is little doubt that 2026 has been a difficult year for the board. The OSM controversy, complaints over evaluation, repeated changes to the language policy and curriculum-related confusion have all put CBSE under scrutiny.
The leadership has also changed considerably. Dharmendra Pradhan resigned as Education Minister in July following the NEET-UG paper leak controversy, with Pralhad Joshi taking over the ministry. At CBSE, Rahul Singh was transferred in June, Lokhande Prashant Sitaram briefly held additional charge, and Mandeep K Bhandari was appointed the new chairperson in September.
Meanwhile, October is ending, but the detailed CBSE Class 10 and Class 12 board examination timetable for 2027 is still awaited . Last year, the tentative schedule was released on September 24, 2025. The board has not announced a reason for the delay this year.
A new leadership team offers an opportunity to restore confidence. But students do not need another announcement promising reform. They need rules that are announced on time, explained properly and, most importantly, stay consistent.
With board examinations approaching, CBSE's biggest task for 2027 should be making its decisions easier to understand, rather than asking students to keep learning new rules along with their textbooks. - Ends Read | Failed in Math, Science or Social Science: CBSE's new rules bring relief for students Read | CBSE drops Class 10 environmental education: New subject choices explained
